passages.happening:
“Wives, in the same way, submit yourselves to your husbands, so that even if they refuse to believe the word, they will be won over without words by the behavior of their wives when they see your pure and reverent demeanor” (verses 1-2).

“Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes, but from the inner disposition of your heart, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious in God’s sight. For this is how the holy women of the past adorned themselves. They put their hope in God and were submissive to their husbands, just as Sarah obeyed Abraham and called him lord. And you are her children if you do what is right and refuse to give way to fear” (verses 3-6).

“Husbands, in the same way, treat your wives with consideration as a delicate vessel, and with honor as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life, so that your prayers will not be hindered” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
‘In the same way’ ties these verses to what came just before: Christ, who suffered without striking back and entrusted himself to God (2:21-25). The household code that began at 2:13 continues.

Peter speaks first to a woman in a hard place: a believing wife whose husband did not believe. In the Roman world a wife was expected to share her husband's religion. One Greek moral writer of the time advised that a wife should worship only her husband's gods and shut the door to strange cults. A wife who had become a Christian on her own was seen as disloyal to her household. The world's advice would have been: give up your faith. Peter does not say that. He tells her to keep her faith and to live it so well that her husband might be won ‘without words’.

Then beauty. In Roman society, elaborate braided hairstyles with gold ornaments were a fashion of wealthy women, and moralists, pagan and Jewish, often criticised such display. Peter points to where real beauty lies: in ‘a gentle and quiet spirit’, which does not fade and which God treasures.

His example is Sarah. In Genesis she speaks of Abraham as ‘my master’, a respectful word for a husband in that culture. And Peter adds a striking phrase: ‘refuse to give way to fear’. These women were living with real risk. Peter wants them to do right and not be ruled by fear.

Then the husbands, and what Peter says to them is about what they owe. Treat your wife ‘with consideration’, with understanding. ‘A delicate vessel’ most likely refers to a woman's lesser physical strength and her weaker legal and social place in that world. And in the same breath Peter calls wives ‘fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life’: equal before God, sharing the same inheritance. A husband who dishonours his wife will find his prayers hindered. God takes her side.
passages.ot:
Peter's example comes from Genesis. When Sarah heard she would have a son in her old age, “she laughed to herself, saying, ‘After I am worn out and my master is old, will I now have this pleasure?’” (Genesis 18:12). ‘My master’ is, in Hebrew, adoni, ‘my lord’, the word behind Peter's ‘called him lord’.

The wisdom books praise the beauty that lasts: “Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised” (Proverbs 31:30).

And the prophets warned husbands who wronged their wives that God was a witness: “the LORD has been a witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have broken faith, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant” (Malachi 2:14).
passages.hard:
Do these verses ask wives to submit to their husbands today? What do Christians agree on, and where do they differ?

Much is agreed. Husband and wife are equally made in God's image and equally saved by grace. Peter calls them ‘fellow heirs’. He speaks to wives as people who answer to God for themselves, and he tells husbands they owe honour and understanding. Beyond that, Christians who share the same faith read these verses differently. It is a question that divides faithful churches, not the faith, and these notes do not choose.

Complementarians hold that men and women are equal in worth but given different callings in marriage, and that a wife's submission to her husband is a lasting pattern, not only a nod to Roman custom. They note that Peter grounds it in the example of Christ and of the holy women of the past, that a husband's headship means self-giving love, not control, and that submission is a wife's own free response, never something a husband may demand or enforce.

Egalitarians hold that men and women are equal in worth and in calling. They read Peter as applying the gospel inside the household customs of his day for the sake of witness, so that unbelieving husbands might be won. They note that Peter's concern is the gospel's good name, that he calls wives ‘fellow heirs’, and that where a partnership of equals no longer brings disgrace, the deeper principle points to mutual submission and a shared inheritance.

Nothing here licenses harshness or abuse. Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. Abuse and other crimes are to be reported to the police and the proper authorities.

If you are being hurt in some other place, at home, at work or in a church, the same is true. Tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: If you are married, ask what your husband or wife sees in you day by day, and whether it draws them toward Christ. Ask where you are giving way to fear. And ask whether you treat your spouse as a fellow heir of the grace of life.

passages.happening:
“Finally, all of you, be like-minded and sympathetic, love as brothers, be tenderhearted and humble. Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with blessing, because to this you were called so that you may inherit a blessing” (verses 8-9).

Then Peter quotes a psalm: “Whoever would love life and see good days must keep his tongue from evil and his lips from deceitful speech. He must turn from evil and do good; he must seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (verses 10-12).
passages.hearers:
‘Finally, all of you.’ Peter has spoken to rulers' subjects, to slaves, to wives and to husbands. Now he speaks to everyone. Five short words describe a church that holds together: of one mind, feeling with one another, loving as family, tender, humble.

Then the hard command. Do not pay back evil for evil, or insult for insult. Pay back blessing. These readers were being insulted by their neighbours. The natural answer was to insult back, or to withdraw in bitterness. Peter says: bless them. That is what Christ did, and it is what believers were ‘called’ to.

The reason is a promise: they will ‘inherit a blessing’. Those who give blessing will receive it.

The psalm Peter quotes says the same. The good life comes by guarding your tongue, turning from evil, and going after peace as if hunting it down. And God sees. His eyes are on those who do right, and his ears are open to them. They do not need to take revenge.
passages.ot:
Peter quotes Psalm 34, the psalm he already echoed in 2:3: “Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from deceitful speech. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it. The eyes of the LORD are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their cry” (Psalm 34:13-15).

Proverbs taught the same refusal of revenge: “Do not say, ‘I will avenge this evil!’ Wait on the LORD, and He will save you” (Proverbs 20:22).
passages.asks: Think of the last time someone insulted you. Ask how you answered. Ask what it would mean to bless that person, in prayer or in a kind word. And ask which of Peter's five words your church most needs from you.

passages.t: Ready to give a reason for your hope
passages.happening:
“Who can harm you if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed. ‘Do not fear what they fear; do not be shaken’” (verses 13-14).

“But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect, keeping a clear conscience, so that those who slander you may be put to shame by your good behavior in Christ. For it is better, if it is God’s will, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil” (verses 15-17).
passages.hearers:
‘Who can harm you?’ does not mean that nothing bad will happen. Peter at once says, ‘even if you should suffer’. He means that no one can take away what truly matters, and that suffering for what is right does not cancel God's blessing.

‘Do not fear what they fear’ comes from Isaiah. Then Peter adds, ‘sanctify Christ as Lord’, set him apart in your hearts as the holy one. In Isaiah those words are about ‘the LORD of Hosts’. Peter gives them to Christ, a quiet confession that Jesus is God.

Then a famous verse. ‘Defense’ is apologia, the word for a speech of defence in a law court, and the root of the English ‘apologetics’. Every believer, not only the clever ones, should be ready to give a reason for their hope, whether to an official or to a curious neighbour.

But how they answer matters as much as what they say: ‘with gentleness and respect’. No sneering, no winning at any cost. A clear conscience and a good life, Peter says, will in time put slander to shame.
passages.ot:
Peter takes his words from Isaiah: “Do not fear what they fear; do not live in dread. The LORD of Hosts is the One you shall regard as holy. Only He should be feared; only He should be dreaded” (Isaiah 8:12-13). In Isaiah's day the people feared an alliance of enemies; God told them to fear him instead.

And the wisdom books join the fear of God with turning from evil: “Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and turn away from evil” (Proverbs 3:7).
passages.hard:
What does it mean to ‘give a defense’ of your hope? Does it mean every Christian has to win arguments?

No. Peter's word means a reasoned answer, the kind given when someone asks. It is not a call to start fights, to corner people, or to treat every conversation as a debate to win. He says the answer should come ‘with gentleness and respect’, and that a good life often speaks before words do.

Some believers feel they must have an answer for every hard question. Peter asks for something simpler and deeper: to know why you hope, and to be ready to say it honestly. It is no failure to say, ‘I do not know, but here is why I trust Christ.’ The site's Honest Answers take up many of the questions people ask, and they try to do it with the respect Peter asks for.
passages.asks: Ask what the reason for your hope is, and whether you could say it in a few honest sentences. Ask whether you answer people with gentleness and respect, especially people who disagree. And ask what you fear, and whether Christ is set apart as Lord in that place.

passages.happening:
“For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God. He was put to death in the body but made alive in the Spirit, in whom He also went and preached to the spirits in prison who disobeyed long ago when God waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built. In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water” (verses 18-20).

“And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also—not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him” (verses 21-22).
passages.hearers:
Peter has told his readers that it is better to suffer for doing good. Now he shows them why, by telling the whole path of Christ.

Christ suffered ‘once for all’: his death does not need to be repeated. He was ‘the righteous for the unrighteous’: he took the place of the guilty. And his goal was ‘to bring you to God’.

Then the path goes on. Put to death in the body, made alive in the Spirit, he ‘went and preached to the spirits in prison’. These are among the hardest words in the New Testament (see below). Then come Noah and the flood. Eight people were saved through the water in the ark, and Peter says that water pictures baptism.

Many scholars think these verses draw on an early Christian hymn or confession. They move step by step: suffered, put to death, made alive, went, preached, raised, gone into heaven, at the right hand. The word ‘went’ appears in verse 19 and again in verse 22 (‘has gone into heaven’), which matters for how some read the passage.

The last line is the point for suffering readers: the Christ they follow went through death to a throne, and every power, ‘angels, authorities, and powers’, is now under him. Those who suffer with him will share his victory.
passages.ot:
The flood story is in Genesis. God saw “that the wickedness of man was great upon the earth” (Genesis 6:5). Noah, his wife, his three sons and their wives went into the ark, eight people (Genesis 7:13). “But God remembered Noah” (Genesis 8:1).

Behind ‘the spirits in prison’ some readers see Genesis 6:1-4, where “the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives whomever they chose” (Genesis 6:2). In 1 Enoch, a Jewish writing widely read in the first century, these sons of God were rebellious angels who were imprisoned. Whether Peter draws on that reading is part of the debate.

Christ at God's right hand fulfils the psalm: “The LORD said to my Lord: ‘Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet’” (Psalm 110:1).
passages.hard:
Who are ‘the spirits in prison’, and what did Christ preach to them? And how does baptism ‘now save’?

The church has read verses 19 and 20 in three main ways. These notes do not choose. One reading, held by Augustine, is that Christ, by the Spirit, preached through Noah to the people of Noah's day, who refused to repent and are now held for judgment. A second holds that between his death and resurrection Christ went to the realm of the dead and proclaimed his message there: some early writers thought of an offer of salvation, others of the freeing of the faithful of old, others of a word of judgment. This reading stands behind the Apostles' Creed's ‘he descended into hell’, whose older sense is ‘descended to the dead’. A third, held by many modern readers, is that the spirits are fallen angels held for their rebellion in Noah's day, and that the risen Christ, on his way to heaven (‘went’ again in verse 22), announced his victory over them. All three agree on Peter's point: Christ's suffering led to triumph over every power. These notes say no more than the text about anyone's state after death.

On baptism, all agree that its power comes from the risen Christ, not the water: ‘not the removal of dirt’. Churches differ on how baptism and salvation are joined. Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran Christians generally hold that God truly gives new life through baptism as his appointed means. Reformed and Presbyterian Christians often speak of it as a sign and seal joined to the reality. Baptists and many other evangelicals see it as the public sign of a salvation already received by faith. ‘Pledge’ is itself debated: an appeal to God for a clean conscience, or a commitment made to God from one. These notes do not choose.
passages.asks: Ask what it means for you that Christ suffered ‘the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God’. If you have been baptised, ask what your baptism says about whose you are. And ask what powers frighten you, and whether you believe they are under Christ.
